title: I Posted the Grain-Mill Hours After They Camped My Numbered Hopper

parts.text: I stepped into mill bay at 5:08 a.m. and baker Inez was already using my numbered hopper. The board said: FORTY MINUTES. HOPPERS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-five, mill steward, holding a clipboard that listed our grind. Inez shrugged. "Bakers keep the stones." I photographed the board, the booking, and her wheat in my hopper. Then I asked for the mill hours. At 5:16 the co-op desk pinged why Inez's wheat sat in our hopper. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The co-op desk can see Inez's wheat in mill bay during our grind.

social.video_title: She camped my numbered grain hopper — Part 1/2
social.description: Grain mill, a baker in my hopper, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the wheat. Would you have asked for the mill hours?

parts.text: Inez called it test grinds until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the hopper still. The hopper went back to my numbered bin. Inez ran a slot of their own and told the next baker atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: BAKERS DO NOT KEEP THE STONES. I keep our grind on a labeled card. Inez brown-bags her wheat. The mill finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Bakers do not keep the stones — Part 2/2
social.description: Mill hours, numbered hopper, and a second line on the board. Were test grinds ever our wheat?
